planting.note: Plant pups or container-grown stock in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, lean soil in full sun; give it plenty of room since it grows faster and larger than most ornamental agaves.

directions: Set pups or nursery plants slightly proud of grade in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; Weber's Agave is one of the largest and fastest-growing commonly cultivated agaves, forming a huge symmetrical rosette of smooth, gray-green to blue-green leaves that lack the marginal teeth found on most agave species, making it a safer choice near walkways and pool decks. It was historically grown in San Luis Potosí, Mexico for pulque and mezcal production and is sometimes confused with Agave americana, which it resembles but outgrows. Like other true agaves it is monocarpic, sending up a tall branched flower stalk after roughly 8-15 years and then dying back while leaving a ring of offsets. Its rapid growth and imposing scale make it a strong choice for large-scale xeriscape beds, medians, and desert-style landscaping where a fast architectural statement is wanted.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock or offsets in spring in well-drained, rocky or sandy soil; unlike most agaves this species tolerates filtered shade and can be tucked under high tree canopy or on north-facing slopes.

directions: Site in sharply drained rocky or gravelly soil, choosing a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade in the hottest climates, since squid agave tolerates more shade than nearly any other agave and can even scorch in relentless reflected sun. Its narrow, arching, spineless leaves curl and twist outward from a stemless rosette in a pattern resembling squid tentacles, and unlike toothed agave species it has no marginal spines, making it a good choice near paths. Native to limestone canyons and cliffs of Nuevo León, Mexico, it spreads slowly by rhizomes into multi-headed clumps rather than relying on a single dramatic bloom-and-die cycle, and produces a comparatively short, dense spike of small yellow-green flowers. Its compact size and shade tolerance make it useful in small gardens, containers, and understory rock plantings where larger agaves would not fit or thrive.

common_name: Macho Mocha Mangave (Giant Speckled Agave-Manfreda Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or nursery divisions in spring into very well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; this hybrid is clonally propagated only, since it does not come true from seed.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, giving it generous room since 'Macho Mocha' is among the largest and most vigorous mangave cultivars, forming a broad rosette of thick, wavy-margined, olive-green leaves heavily speckled with maroon-burgundy spots that intensify in bright light and cool weather. As a hybrid between Agave and Manfreda parentage it inherits the softer, more pliable leaves and hummingbird-pollinated flower spikes of manfreda along with the bold rosette form of agave, and importantly it is polycarpic, meaning the rosette survives flowering rather than dying like a true century plant. It grows considerably faster than pure agave species, reaching full size in just a few seasons, and has become a popular large-scale accent for Gulf South and Texas xeriscape beds and containers. Sharp drainage and good air movement are essential, since rot from wet soil is the primary risk to an otherwise low-maintenance plant.

common_name: Brakelights Red Yucca (Compact Deep-Red Hesperaloe Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; its compact, uniform habit makes it ideal for mass planting along walkways, medians, and small residential beds where the straight species would be too large.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun, spacing plants for a tidy, uniform mass planting since 'Brakelights' is a selected dwarf sport of red yucca that stays roughly half the size of the species. It forms a dense rosette of narrow, fibrous-edged, blue-green leaves and produces shorter, more compact flower spikes packed with intensely deep red-orange tubular blooms nearly continuously from spring through fall, making it one of the most reliable long-season hummingbird plants for hot climates. Like the species it is extraordinarily heat and drought tolerant, deer resistant, and unfussy about soil as long as drainage is sharp, but its smaller, denser form fits parking lot islands, foundation plantings, and small residential xeriscapes where the taller straight species would overwhelm the space. Being a patented selection, it is propagated only by division rather than seed, ensuring uniform color and size.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to part shade; protect from hard freeze and avoid overhead watering, which can rot the tight rosette center.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright sun to light shade, letting the soil dry fully between waterings. Echeveria agavoides forms an unusually geometric, tightly packed rosette of thick, pointed, wax-textured leaves that look more like a miniature agave than a typical echeveria, giving rise to its common name, and the leaf tips flush deep red to maroon under bright light and cool temperatures, earning the nickname lipstick echeveria. In spring it sends up slender, arching stems of coral-pink, yellow-tipped bell flowers that draw hummingbirds and small pollinators. It is one of the most important parent species behind many modern hybrid echeveria cultivars prized for crisp rosette form, and it performs well outdoors in warm, humid Gulf South summers as long as drainage is sharp, though it should be moved under cover or into a greenhouse before hard freezes.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Chocolate Chips Manfreda (Wavy-Leaf Mottled Manfreda Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in part shade to full sun; light afternoon shade in the hottest climates helps preserve the deep chocolate-maroon leaf mottling.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in part shade to full sun, where its low rosette of soft, undulating, gray-green leaves heavily blotched with dark chocolate-maroon spots forms a striking groundcover-scale accent along the front of a xeric bed. In summer it sends up a tall, slender, branching spike of small, greenish-brown, tubular flowers with a sweet, spicy fragrance that intensifies at dusk, attracting hawk moths and hummingbirds much like its wild manfreda relatives. Selected and introduced by a Texas specialty nursery, this cultivar has become a favored parent in mangave breeding programs for its distinctive spotting and soft, non-spiny leaf texture, and it works equally well massed as a small-scale xeric groundcover or grown as a specimen in raised beds and containers. Sharp drainage is essential since, like other manfredas, it is prone to rot in heavy or poorly drained soil.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown stock in spring in extremely well-drained, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; this species is less cold-hardy than many ornamental agaves, so site it where winter drainage is fastest and coldest air does not pool.

directions: Site in extremely fast-draining, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; Agave colorata is prized for its thick, broad, undulating blue-gray leaves marked with distinctive bud printing, the cross-hatched imprint patterns left on the leaf surface where adjacent leaves pressed together while still folded in the bud. Widely spaced marginal teeth and a stout dark terminal spine give it strong architectural presence despite its relatively compact, rounded rosette form compared to larger agave species. Native to the coastal thornscrub and desert of Sonora, Mexico, it is highly heat and drought tolerant but somewhat less cold-hardy than agaves from higher-elevation Chihuahuan Desert habitat, so it is best suited to the warmer end of zone 7-10 gardens. Like most agaves it is monocarpic, flowering once on a tall stalk after many years then dying back while leaving offsets to continue the planting.
